title: How Olympic Gold Quest Built India's Medal Machine From a Coffee Shop to 400 Athletes
excerpt: Founded by legends Geet Sethi and Prakash Padukone, OGQ has supported athletes behind 13 of India's 21 Olympic medals since 2012 — and is now targeting the 2036 Games.
body:
• Olympic Gold Quest, a non-profit founded in 2000 by Geet Sethi and Prakash Padukone, now supports close to 400 athletes across 10 Olympic and 8 Paralympic sports
  • Athletes backed by OGQ won 13 of India's 21 Olympic medals from London 2012 through Paris 2024, and 35 of 48 Paralympic medals at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024
  • The organization is already scouting and preparing athletes with medal potential for LA 2028 and the 2036 Games, which India is bidding to host

When Geet Sethi walked out of the 1998 Asian Games in Bangkok, the former world billiards champion knew something was structurally wrong with Indian sport. Athletes with genuine talent were losing not because they lacked ability, but because no system existed to give them world-class coaching, nutrition, sports science, and logistical support. Two years later, he and former All England badminton champion Prakash Padukone founded Olympic Gold Quest — a non-profit that has since become arguably the most consequential private organization in Indian sport.

From One Athlete to Nearly 400

OGQ's journey from concept to institution is a case study in patient institution-building. In its early years, the organization operated without an office — meetings happened at coffee shops, as former India hockey captain and OGQ CEO Viren Rasquinha has recounted. Corporate board members including Niraj Bajaj and Shitin Desai helped secure initial funding, and in 2007, OGQ took on its first athlete: shooter Gagan Narang, just before the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PwihwLKaMHw

From that single athlete, OGQ has grown to support close to 400 athletes across 10 Olympic sports — including badminton, boxing, shooting, archery, and wrestling — and 8 Paralympic disciplines, according to Forbes India. Neha Aggarwal, OGQ's chief partnerships officer and a table tennis Olympian herself, described the organization's approach as deeply customized: physiotherapists, nutritionists, fitness trainers, and mental conditioning coaches work around the clock with athletes at their training locations.

"It's a golden period to be an athlete in India."

— Neha Aggarwal, OGQ Chief Partnerships Officer, speaking to Forbes India

The Medal Count Speaks

The numbers tell a compelling story. OGQ-supported athletes accounted for 13 of India's 21 Olympic medals across the last four Games — from London 2012 through Paris 2024, according to Grokipedia's analysis. At the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, 10 of India's 19 medal winners were OGQ-backed. At Paris 2024, 49 OGQ-supported athletes competed in the Olympics (four won medals), and 54 competed in the Paralympics (25 won medals).

The organization has also facilitated 66 junior world championship titles, underlining its emphasis on long-term pipeline development rather than short-term medal chasing.

The LA 2028 Playbook

OGQ's preparation for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics is already well advanced. Aggarwal told Forbes India that the foundation had identified medal-potential athletes for LA 2028 more than two years before the Games and is now focused on "conversion" — turning medal-probable candidates into actual medalists through incremental improvements across training, competition exposure, and sports science.

India's performance at Paris 2024 informs the strategy. The country won six medals but had six fourth-place finishes and multiple close quarterfinal losses. Aggarwal called Paris "an Olympic of missed opportunities," noting there were 15 realistic medal chances and only six conversions.

Looking Toward 2036

The broader context for OGQ's work is India's bid to host the 2036 Olympics. If successful, the country would face enormous pressure to deliver a competitive home medal tally. OGQ's two-decade track record of systematic athlete development — funded largely through corporate partnerships with organizations like HCL and supported by diaspora philanthropy, including fundraising events in US cities like Boston — positions it as a critical piece of that ambition.

The organization that started in a coffee shop now operates at the intersection of Indian sport, corporate India, and global diaspora engagement. The question for the next decade is whether India's institutional infrastructure can scale to match the ambition that OGQ has been quietly building since 2000.
